body_text: CARMEL, Ind. (June 10, 2026) —Leading national financial services provider Merchants Capital today announced more than $33.8 million for the construction and permanent financing of Village of Valor, a 54-unit affordable housing community in Palm Springs, Fla. developed by Turnstone Development and Faith Hope Love Charity, Inc. Village of Valor will provide housing for military veterans and their families. Merchants Capital secured a $6.5 million Freddie Mac Forward TEL permanent loan and a $15.8 million construction loan provided by Merchants Bank for the development. Merchants Capital also provided $11.5 million in low-income housing tax credit (LIHTC) equity as the syndicator. “Village of Valor will provide much needed housing for military veterans, but it will also address specific needs of this community,” said Lee Oller, Executive Vice President of Originations at Merchants Capital. “As a financing partner, we appreciate the opportunity to collaborate with partners on this comprehensive initiative dedicated to honoring and serving veterans.” “Village of Valor will provide much needed housing for military veterans, but it will also address specific needs of this community. As a financing partner, we appreciate the opportunity to collaborate with partners on this comprehensive initiative dedicated to honoring and serving veterans.” Lee Oller EVP, Originations The development will offer 26 two-bedroom apartments and 28 three-bedroom apartments. Half of the units will be set aside for residents below 50% area median income (AMI) and six units will be set aside for persons with special needs. “Village of Valor has been thoughtfully designed to provide affordable housing, accommodate military families with larger apartments and foster community inherent among veterans,” said Josh Reed, Executive Vice President of LIHTC Acquisitions at Merchants Capital. “We look forward to seeing the impact of this holistic development.” “Village of Valor has been thoughtfully designed to provide affordable housing, accommodate military families with larger apartments and foster community inherent among veterans. We look forward to seeing the impact of this holistic development.” Josh Reed EVP & Head of Acquisitions, Equity Investments Designed as a community to support veterans and improve quality-of-life after military service, Village of Valor will feature energy-efficient units housed in two four-story buildings. Unit interiors will include washer/dryer connections, energy efficient stainless-steel appliances, ceiling fans and individual porches or balconies. Turnstone Development Corporation has developed more than 2,400 affordable housing units and leveraged more than $350 million in private and public investment capital sources. Turnstone Development Corporation is a not-for-profit that creates and preserves affordable housing. Faith Hope Love Charity, Inc. is also a not-for-profit that brings expertise in working with military veterans and their families and connecting them to supportive services. “Turnstone is so proud to be involved in the development of Village of Valor. This development isn’t just housing—it’s a place where veterans can rebuild, connect and thrive in the community they so proudly served,” said Sue Wiemer, Executive Director of Turnstone Development. “We know that affordable housing will meet an initial need, but through the supportive services provided by our development partner Faith Hope Love Charity, we collectively are excited to introduce services designed to support and benefit our veterans.” “Faith, Hope, Love, Charity, Inc. was founded over thirty years ago by two formerly homeless veterans who wanted to make things better for the veterans coming up behind them. The Village of Valor represents an exciting step in our Founder Roy Foster’s vision and the mission of our agency to reintegrate homeless and at-risk veterans and their families back into the community to sustain independent living,” said Joshua W. Maddock, Executive Director of Faith, Hope, Love, Charity, Inc. “The supportive services on site at the Village of Valor will help restore our veterans’ dignity and provide them and their families with hope and the opportunity to thrive. We at Faith, Hope, Love, Charity, Inc. are thrilled to join with our development partner Turnstone Development to bring much needed affordable housing to Palm Beach County, Florida.” Community amenities will include recreational areas, a picnic area, walking paths, a basketball court, pickleball and a swimming pool. Commercial and office space will be located on the ground floor of one of the buildings for philanthropic efforts related to military veterans and their families. Construction began in April 2026 and is expected to be completed in 18 months. To learn more about Merchants Capital and its services, visit www.MerchantsCapital.com or find Merchants Capital on Facebook , X , LinkedIn and Instagram . Share

(Nasdaq: AERT) (“Aeries” or the “Company”), a global leader in AI-powered business transformation and Global Capability Center (“GCC”) services, today highlighted the significance of its financial progress and strategic positioning at a critical market inflection point. The Financial Turnaround With $70 million in revenue, Aeries delivered substantial improvements in profitability and cash generation. The Company returned to profitability, reporting net income of $3.5 million, compared with a net loss of $(21.6) million in fiscal year 2025. This represents an improvement of more than $25 million year over year. Adjusted EBITDA reached $8.3 million, exceeding the Company's increased guidance range of $7.0 million to $8.0 million. The Adjusted EBITDA margin expanded by 18.5 percentage points to 11.9%, up from (6.6)% in the prior year. Importantly, these results were achieved while the Company continued to invest in AI-enabled capabilities, client expansion, and platform innovation. Operating cash flow improved to $6.8 million, up from $(1.0) million used in operations in fiscal year 2025, marking the fourth consecutive quarter of positive operating cash flow. SG&A expenses declined 72% year-over-year to $12.8 million from $45.5 million, reflecting a significantly leaner and more scalable operating structure. Positioned in an Accelerating Market Private equity sponsors and mid-market enterprises are rapidly adopting GCC operating models that embed AI and automation as core design elements. Demand for AI-embedded GCC models is accelerating beyond pilot programs. Clients are asking: “How do we build a GCC that operates with AI as a native?” Management believes these forces are creating a significant opportunity for PE-backed enterprises evaluating GCC transformation partners. Aeries is positioned at the center of this inflection, with a portfolio of signed contracts and expanding client relationships. We delivered $70 million in revenue, exceeded our increased Adjusted EBITDA guidance, generated positive operating cash flow for four consecutive quarters, and returned to profitability, all while continuing to invest in AI-enabled capabilities and client expansion. “What excites us most is what we're seeing in the market right now. Private equity sponsors are actively evaluating GCC transformation partners. Demand for AI-embedded GCC models is accelerating. Leveraging advanced technologies, automation, and scalable global delivery models, Aeries provides tailored GCC and transformation solutions designed to support long-term operational efficiency and enterprise value creation. Founded in 2012, Aeries Technology supports clients through its India and Mexico delivery operations and continues to focus on scalable GCC-led transformation programs for private equity-backed and mid-market enterprises. The Company uses non-GAAP financial measures to budget, make operating and strategic decisions, and evaluate its performance. The Company has detailed the non-GAAP adjustments that it makes in the non-GAAP definitions below. The adjustments generally fall within the categories of non-cash items. The Company believes the non-GAAP measures presented herein should always be considered along with, and not as a substitute for or superior to, the related GAAP financial measures. For further information, see “Reconciliation of Non—GAAP Financial Measures” below, including the reconciliations of these non-GAAP measures to their most directly comparable GAAP financial measures. The Company defines Adjusted EBITDA as net income (loss) before interest, income taxes, depreciation and amortization, further adjusted to exclude stock-based compensation, M&A transaction-related costs, severance pay, and changes in fair value of derivative liabilities. 1612879829.1 Adjusted EBITDA is a key performance indicator the Company uses in evaluating our operating performance and in making financial, operating, and planning decisions. The Company believes this measure is useful to investors in the evaluation of Aeries’ operating performance as such information was used by the Company’s management for internal reporting and planning procedures, including aspects of our consolidated operating budget and capital expenditures. Adjusted EBITDA as a measure has some limitations in that it does not reflect: (i) our cash expenditures or future requirements for capital expenditures or contractual commitments; (ii) foreign exchange gain/loss; (iii) changes in, or cash requirements for, working capital; (iv) significant interest expense or the cash requirements necessary to service interest or principal payments on our outstanding debt; (v) payments made or future requirements for income taxes; (vi) cash requirements for future replacement or payment in depreciated or amortized assets; (vii) stock based compensation costs, (viii) severance pay, (ix) Business Combination and M&A transaction related costs, which represent non-recurring legal, professional, personnel and other fees and expenses incurred in connection with potential mergers and acquisitions related activities, and (x) change in fair value of derivative liabilities. title: The self-maintaining knowledge base
summary: Slite is the self-maintaining AI knowledge base that stays accurate. Verified by your team, synced with your tools, trusted by every agent.
body_text: Meet the all-new Slite: the first self-maintaining knowledge base . It pairs a structured, verified knowledge base with an AI agent that detects when documentation has drifted from reality, proposes the fix, and routes every change through human approval before it becomes truth. The Slite Agent Slite Agent is now available on the Pro plan. It detects when docs drift from reality across 20+ connected tools, proposes fixes, and routes every change through human review before anything is applied. New global floating agent panel (three states: collapsed, popover, expanded) that persists across doc navigation Triage view in the sidebar: a dedicated mode showing all pending agent runs with unread badges and per-row indicators Agent approval right panel: click an approval card to open a 50/50 split view with the full-document diff, a minimap to jump between change hotspots, and Accept/Dismiss controls Redesigned approval cards for all agent action types (edit, create, rename, archive, ownership change) Improved diff rendering: inline diffs, correct handling of mentions, code, links, and tables Agent thread titles now reflect the document being worked on (e.g. "Fact Check the Reimbursement Policy") Slite Agent is callable via Slite UI, Slack, Claude, MCP, API, and the verification popover Scheduled automations: set up nightly routines to review entire doc channels and wake up to a triage queue Track every edit origin Slite now tracks whether a doc edit, comment, or action was made from the app, desktop, mobile, public API, MCP, or the Slite Agent. The Activity Log displays it, and three months of history have been backfilled. New plans, pricing, and credit system Standard → Basic ($10/user/month), Knowledge Suite → Pro ($20/user/month) Pro includes 50 monthly credits per seat for agent actions; credits are pooled at the workspace level 14-day free trial (no credit card required) replaces the old free plan MCP access now included on all plans, including Basic New AI usage screen in settings: see credits spent per user with a custom date range picker New slite.com The Slite website has been completely redesigned with a new homepage hero featuring an animated agent demo, Slite Agent and MCP sections, bento layouts, and full mobile responsiveness. Other improvements Via attribution badges on comments: a badge next to the avatar indicates when a comment was created, resolved, or archived via MCP or API Cmd+Shift+O now opens the Slite Agent directly Restored org ownership transfer in the app Mobile: collection view sorts now respected; mentioned-user avatars in database columns now resolve correctly MCP SliteML format is now MDX-compatible for programmatic parsing Onboarding flows updated: better UI, no duplicate steps between Slite and Agent onboarding Super Help Center merged into the Slite Help Center Bug fixes Fixed cited PDF sources from Ask not opening the source document Fixed Claude logo not showing on MCP OAuth consent screen Fixed incorrect triage URL returned by MCP Fixed citations not flowing back from Slite child agent to Super Fixed Asana project picker showing inaccessible root nodes Fixed long group names overflowing in settings Fixed doc insights not loading when a doc has a reaction Fixed collaboration crash on missing history (now falls back to current snapshot)

title: Linux MDM for Developer Workstations
summary: Linux MDM for Developer Workstations
body_text: Developer workstations are some of the highest-value targets on any corporate network. They hold source code, database credentials, cloud infrastructure access keys, API tokens, SSH private keys, and often direct access to production systems. A compromised developer laptop doesn't just expose one person's email — it can give an attacker a path into your entire software supply chain. That makes securing developer endpoints a serious priority. But developers also need freedom to install tools, run containers, compile code, and experiment with configurations that would make a compliance officer nervous. The tension between security and productivity is real, and it's where most organizations either over-restrict and lose engineering trust, or under-restrict and accept risk they shouldn't. This article covers how to manage that tension using MDM. If you need background on what MDM is, start with What is MDM? . For compliance-specific implementation, see the Linux MDM compliance guide . For security architecture and incident response, the Linux MDM security guide goes into detail. Why Developer Workstations Are Different General-purpose corporate endpoints — the machines used by sales, HR, marketing — typically run a browser, an office suite, and a few SaaS tools. Locking those down is straightforward. Developer workstations are different. Engineers routinely need root or sudo access. They install packages from multiple sources. They run local servers, databases, and container runtimes. They SSH into remote infrastructure and interact with version control systems containing proprietary code, often across multiple projects with different technology stacks simultaneously. Applying the same MDM policies to developer machines that you apply to general staff creates friction that slows engineering work. When a developer can't install a build dependency without filing an IT ticket and waiting two days, they find workarounds. Those workarounds — personal machines, unmanaged VMs, shadow IT accounts — are almost always less secure than whatever you were trying to prevent. Good MDM strategy for developers builds policies that protect the organization without creating incentives to circumvent them. Role-Based Policies That Actually Work The answer isn't a single policy tier. It's role-based differentiation. Your MDM platform should let you define policy groups that reflect how different teams use their machines. A frontend developer working in JavaScript has a different risk profile than a platform engineer managing Kubernetes clusters. A data scientist running Python environments has different needs than a security engineer running penetration testing tools. At minimum, separate developer endpoints from general corporate endpoints in your policy groups. Within the developer tier, consider further segmentation based on infrastructure access level. Engineers with production access should have stricter posture requirements — full disk encryption verified, firewall active, OS fully patched, SSH keys meeting minimum length requirements — than engineers who only touch staging environments. The goal is proportional security: tighter controls where the risk is higher, more flexibility where the blast radius is smaller. Security Without Surveillance Developers push back on MDM for understandable reasons. Nobody wants their employer watching their screen, logging their keystrokes, or tracking which applications they use throughout the day. The good news is that effective endpoint security doesn't require any of that. The distinction that matters is between device posture checks and user behavior monitoring. Device posture is about the state of the machine: Is the disk encrypted? Is the firewall enabled? Are OS patches current? Is the MDM agent running? These are binary, verifiable conditions that don't involve looking at what the person is doing. You can enforce strong security posture without collecting browsing history, taking screenshots, or logging application usage. Making this distinction explicit during rollout matters. Tell your engineering team exactly what the agent checks and what it doesn't. Publish the policy. Let people audit it. Transparency builds trust, and trust makes adoption smoother. When developers understand the agent is checking whether LUKS encryption is active rather than watching their terminal sessions, most objections disappear. Managing Development Tools Through MDM Developers install a lot of software. Package managers are the primary channel — apt and yum for system packages, npm and pip and cargo for language-specific dependencies, Homebrew or Nix for supplementary tooling. IDEs like VS Code, JetBrains products, and Neovim with extensive plugin ecosystems add another layer. Shell environments with custom dotfiles, terminal multiplexers, and CLI utilities round things out. MDM can manage this without micromanaging it. The practical approach is to maintain approved repositories and registries rather than approved package lists. Allow developers to install what they need from sources you trust, block installations from sources you don't, and scan installed packages for known vulnerabilities on a regular schedule. This gives engineers freedom to choose their tools while maintaining visibility into what's running across your fleet. For system-level packages, enforce GPG signature verification on apt and yum repositories. For language-specific package managers, consider running internal mirrors or proxies (like Artifactory or Nexus) that cache approved packages and block known-malicious ones. MDM policies can ensure these mirrors are configured as the default source on every developer machine and that direct access to public registries is either proxied or restricted. Shell environment management is lighter-touch. You generally don't want to dictate someone's .bashrc or .zshrc. But you do want to ensure that certain security-relevant configurations — like SSH agent forwarding restrictions or GPG agent settings — are present. MDM can deploy baseline dotfile fragments that coexist with personal customization. Container and Runtime Security Most developer workstations run Docker, and many run local Kubernetes clusters through tools like minikube, kind, or k3d. Containers introduce a distinct attack surface that your MDM policies need to address. Start with the Docker daemon configuration. Rootless mode should be the default for developer workstations. Running Docker as root means any container escape gives the attacker root on the host. Rootless Docker eliminates that escalation path. MDM can enforce the daemon.json configuration to require rootless mode, enable seccomp profiles that restrict system calls available to containers, and configure user namespace remapping so container processes map to unprivileged host UIDs. Image governance is the next layer. Developers pull container images from Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, cloud provider registries, and occasionally random URLs from blog posts. MDM policies should define approved registries and block pulls from unapproved sources. Pair this with vulnerability scanning — tools like Trivy or Grype can run locally and flag images with critical CVEs before they're used in development. For local Kubernetes clusters, the main concern is preventing configurations that affect the host system. Ensure that local clusters don't bind to external network interfaces, don't mount sensitive host paths, and don't run with elevated privileges unless explicitly required for testing. Developer Credential and Key Management SSH keys are the most common authentication mechanism for developers accessing remote systems. They're also one of the most commonly mismanaged. Keys without passphrases, keys that haven't been rotated in years, keys with insufficient bit lengths, and keys scattered across multiple machines without any inventory — this is the norm at most organizations. MDM gives you a way to enforce SSH key hygiene at scale. Policies can require minimum key lengths (4096-bit RSA or Ed25519), verify that private keys are passphrase-protected, and flag keys that exceed your rotation window. Some platforms can inventory SSH public keys across your fleet, useful for identifying orphaned keys that still grant infrastructure access after someone changes roles or leaves. Secret detection is equally important. Developers accidentally commit API keys, database passwords, and access tokens to git repositories with alarming regularity. Pre-commit hooks that scan for high-entropy strings and known secret patterns catch most of these before they reach a shared repository. MDM can deploy these hooks across every developer machine, ensuring consistent coverage rather than relying on individual engineers to install them. GPG commit signing is worth enabling fleet-wide. Signed commits create a verifiable chain of authorship in your codebase. If an attacker compromises a developer's account and pushes malicious code, unsigned commits stand out immediately. MDM can manage GPG key provisioning, ensure signing is enabled in git configs, and enforce that your repositories require signed commits. Securing CI/CD From the Endpoint The CI/CD pipeline doesn't start on the build server. It starts on the developer's machine, where code is written, tested locally, and pushed. If that machine is compromised, the attacker can inject malicious code before it ever reaches your pipeline's security gates. Build environment standardization helps. MDM can ensure developer machines use consistent compiler versions, dependency versions, and build tool configurations. This reduces "works on my machine" issues and limits the attack surface — a standardized environment is easier to monitor for anomalies than a fragmented one. Pipeline credential storage deserves attention. Developers should never have CI/CD tokens or deployment credentials stored in plaintext on their local machines. MDM policies can scan for common credential storage locations — environment variables in shell profiles, .env files, CI config files — and flag insecure storage. Push teams toward credential managers or short-lived tokens fetched at runtime rather than persisted to disk. Pre-commit hooks serve double duty here. Beyond secret detection, they can enforce formatting standards, run linting, and verify commits meet team conventions. MDM deployment ensures every developer has the same hooks without relying on documentation that nobody reads. For more on keeping systems updated alongside these controls, see the Linux MDM patch management guide . Device Ownership Models and Lifecycle The question of corporate-owned versus BYOD matters more for developers than for most other roles. Developers on personal machines are harder to secure, harder to offboard, and harder to audit. But some organizations — especially those hiring contractors or remote engineers in regions where shipping hardware is complicated — need to support BYOD. For corporate-owned devices, MDM should handle provisioning end to end. A new engineer powers on a laptop and the enrollment process configures everything: disk encryption, firewall rules, approved repositories, SSH key generation, GPG key provisioning, Docker daemon configuration, IDE installation, and baseline dotfiles. This should take minutes, not days. Automation here reduces time-to-productivity and eliminates configuration drift from the start. BYOD requires a different approach. You can't wipe a personal machine or enforce system-level policies as aggressively. Consider containerized work environments — VMs or isolated workspaces that keep corporate code and credentials separate from personal data. The MDM agent monitors the work environment without touching personal files. It comes with tradeoffs in performance and developer experience, but it works for organizations that need the flexibility. Offboarding is where gaps tend to appear. When a developer leaves, you need to revoke access comprehensively: SSH keys removed from servers, GPG keys revoked, git tokens invalidated, VPN certificates revoked, cloud IAM credentials deactivated, and the device wiped (corporate-owned) or work container destroyed (BYOD). MDM platforms like Swif.ai can automate this sequence, triggering a full offboarding workflow from a single action rather than relying on a manual checklist someone inevitably misses a step on. Practical Next Steps If you're starting from scratch, begin with an inventory. Know how many developer workstations you have, what Linux distributions they run, and what tools are installed. You can't secure what you can't see. From there, prioritize in this order: - Full disk encryption enforced on every machine - SSH key hygiene policies (minimum key length, passphrase requirement, rotation schedule) - Docker daemon configuration (rootless mode, seccomp profiles) - Approved package registries and vulnerability scanning - Pre-commit hooks for secret detection deployed fleet-wide - GPG commit signing enabled across engineering teams - Automated provisioning and offboarding workflows Start with items that reduce the most risk with the least friction. Disk encryption and SSH key policies are high-impact and low-disruption. Docker configuration and registry restrictions require more coordination but close significant gaps. Pre-commit hooks and GPG signing are adoption challenges more than technical ones — get engineering leadership bought in before rolling them out. Measure what you enforce. Track the percentage of developer machines meeting posture requirements, secrets caught by pre-commit hooks, average time to provision a new machine, and completeness of your offboarding process. These metrics tell you whether your MDM deployment is actually improving security or just generating dashboard data nobody acts on.

body_text: What Is Stress in Mechanics Stress in mechanics is the internal force per unit area that a material develops in response to an externally applied load or constraint. The atoms and molecules within the material resist displacement by generating opposing internal forces distributed across the loaded cross-section when a force acts on a body. Stress is expressed mathematically as force divided by area and is measured in pascals (Pa) or pounds per square inch (psi). A steel rod with a cross-sectional area of 100 mm² carrying an axial tensile load of 50,000 N develops a 500 MPa only if the axial load is concentric and the section is uniform. Stress is distinct from strain, which measures the geometric deformation that accompanies the stress state. The relationship between stress and strain defines a material's mechanical behavior, including its stiffness, ductility, and capacity to absorb energy before fracture. Understanding stress is foundational to every structural and mechanical calculation in engineering practice. What Defines Stress at the Atomic Level? At the atomic level, stress is defined by the interatomic or intermolecular forces that resist changes in the equilibrium spacing of atoms within a crystalline or amorphous lattice. Under elastic loading, atoms are displaced slightly from equilibrium; under plastic deformation, permanent deformation mainly occurs by dislocation motion, and the attractive forces holding the lattice together generate a restoring force proportional to the displacement. The magnitude of the restoring force per unit area of the atomic plane corresponds directly to the macroscopic stress measured by an engineer. FCC metals are generally ductile because their crystal structure provides many active slip systems, not because the atomic bonds themselves are ductile. Body-centered cubic (BCC) metals (iron, tungsten, chromium) exhibit higher theoretical shear strength but are more susceptible to cleavage fracture under low-temperature loading. The elastic modulus, which quantifies a material's stiffness, reflects the curvature of the interatomic potential energy curve near the equilibrium spacing. A steeper potential energy curve produces a higher elastic modulus, directly linking atomic bonding character to macroscopic mechanical elasticity. Is Stress Caused by Internal Forces Between Particles? Yes, stress is caused by internal forces acting from particle to particle within a material. Equilibrium requires that the internal particles generate equal and opposite forces to resist deformation when an external force is applied to a solid body. The stress at any given plane equals that internal force divided by the plane's area in a tensile test specimen. Every cross-sectional plane carries a distributed internal force that balances the applied end load. The consequence is direct at the engineering scale, a material fails when the internal particle-level forces exceed the cohesive strength of the atomic bonds. Particle-level bond rupture occurs suddenly with little prior deformation in brittle ceramics (glass, alumina), making stress concentration at crack tips particularly dangerous. Particles redistribute load through plastic slip before final fracture in ductile metals (low-carbon steel, annealed copper), giving engineers a visible warning before complete failure. The particle-level origin of stress is therefore the physical basis for every engineering design limit. What Is the Importance of Stress of Materials? The importance of stress in materials lies in its direct control over whether a component survives or fails under real-world loading conditions. Every engineered structure carries a defined stress state during operation, and exceeding the material's allowable stress at any location leads to yielding, cracking, or catastrophic fracture. Stress governs the selection of materials for a given application. A titanium alloy with a yield strength of 880 MPa is chosen for aerospace fasteners precisely because the stress demand exceeds what aluminum or polymer fasteners withstand. Stress analysis also determines wall thicknesses in pressure vessels, cross-sectional dimensions in structural beams, and case-hardening depths in gear teeth. Engineers would rely entirely on trial-and-error prototyping without quantifying stress, increasing development time and material waste. The financial consequence of stress-related failures is substantial. A single structural failure in infrastructure (bridges, pipelines, pressure equipment) generates repair and liability costs that reach millions of dollars. Accurate stress evaluation, applied during the design phase, is the most cost-effective safeguard against premature component failure across civil, mechanical, and aerospace engineering disciplines. Why Is Stress Analysis Critical in Engineering Design? Stress analysis is critical in engineering design because it identifies the locations and magnitudes of peak internal forces before a structure is built or a part is manufactured. Finite element analysis (FEA), for example, divides a complex geometry into thousands of discrete elements and computes the stress state at each node, revealing stress concentrations at fillets, holes, and abrupt section changes that hand calculations may overlook. A stress concentration factor (Kt) at a sharp internal corner in a machine part can reach 3.0 or higher, meaning the local stress is 3 times the nominal value calculated from simple formulas. Identifying that concentration early allows a designer to increase the fillet radius, change the material, or reduce the applied load before a fatigue crack initiates. Governing codes (ASME, FAA, ISO 13485) ASME pressure-vessel rules and FAA aircraft certification often require structural substantiation/analysis; ISO 13485 is a quality management standard and does not itself specifically mandate stress analysis for all medical implants. Stress analysis is, therefore, not a supplementary check but a required deliverable that directly protects both public safety and design certification. How Does Stress in Mechanics Work? Stress in mechanics works by distributing an applied external force over the internal cross-sectional area of a body, creating a field of internal forces that vary in magnitude and direction throughout the material. The normal stress across any perpendicular plane equals 200 MPa when a tensile load of 100 kN is applied to a rod with a uniform cross-section of 500 mm², uniform stress requires a prismatic/uniform cross-section and concentric axial loading; isotropy is not the main condition. The stress field distorts at geometric discontinuities (notches, holes, threads), and peak stresses concentrate locally while surrounding regions carry less. Stress is described mathematically using a 3x3 tensor that captures normal stress components on three orthogonal planes and shear stress components on each of the planes, totaling 9 components (reduced to 6 independent values by symmetry). The principal stresses, derived from the stress tensor, identify the maximum and minimum normal stresses acting on planes where shear stress vanishes. Engineers use principal stress values to apply failure criteria (von Mises, Tresca, maximum normal stress) that predict whether a material will yield or fracture. What Is the Use of Stress in Mechanics? The use of Stress in Mechanics are listed below. Structural Safety Verification : Stress calculations confirm that every structural member (beams, columns, shells, fasteners) carries loads within its allowable stress limit, preventing yielding or fracture. Building codes (AISC, ACI, Eurocode) define allowable stress values for common structural materials, providing a direct benchmark for design compliance. Material Selection : Comparing the maximum stress demand of an application to the yield and ultimate strengths of candidate materials narrows the selection to those that perform reliably. A landing gear component experiencing peak stresses of 700 MPa requires a high-strength steel or titanium alloy rather than a standard aluminum grade. Fatigue Life Prediction : Cyclic stress amplitude and mean stress levels are the primary inputs to S-N (stress-life) curves, which predict the number of load cycles a component withstands before crack initiation. A rotating shaft designed for 10⁸ cycles at a stress amplitude below the endurance limit avoids fatigue failure indefinitely under ideal conditions. Thermal Stress Management : Stress analysis identifies regions where differential thermal expansion generates internal stresses in assemblies (bimetallic strips, engine cylinder heads, printed circuit boards). Managing thermal stress prevents delamination, warping, and cracking in temperature-cycling environments. Manufacturing Process Control : Residual stresses introduced by welding, machining, casting, and heat treatment are quantified through stress analysis to prevent distortion, stress-corrosion cracking, or premature fatigue failure in finished parts. Shot peening, for example, intentionally introduces compressive residual stress of 200 MPa to 700 MPa at the surface to extend fatigue life. Failure Investigation : Post-failure stress analysis reconstructs the loading history and identifies the origin of the fracture, supporting root cause analysis and redesign. Fractographic evidence combined with stress modeling pinpoints whether overload, fatigue, stress corrosion, or creep initiated the failure. Seismic and Dynamic Load Analysis : Stress analysis is crucial in designing structures to withstand dynamic forces, such as earthquakes or wind loads. It ensures that the structure resists peak stresses during dynamic events without failing. Composite Material Design : Stress analysis helps determine how different layers or fibers interact under load for materials like carbon fiber composites, ensuring optimal strength and stiffness without compromising on weight. Stress distribution within composites is essential for maximizing performance in aerospace, automotive, and sporting equipment. Pressure Vessel and Pipe Design : Stress analysis ensures that vessels and pipes, especially those subject to high internal pressures, are designed to withstand the resulting stresses. It helps prevent catastrophic failures like ruptures or leaks by determining the appropriate thickness and material for the walls. Bridge and Infrastructure Design : Stress analysis plays a critical role in designing bridges, tunnels, and other infrastructures, ensuring that the structures safely carry the weight of vehicles, pedestrians, and environmental loads over extended periods. Wear and Tear Prediction: Stress analysis can help identify contact pressure and deformation zones related to wear, but wear prediction also requires tribology, lubrication, surface roughness, hardness, and sliding conditions. It is possible to design components that minimize wear and extend operational life by understanding stress distribution. Cryogenic and High-Temperature Applications : Stress analysis aids in the design of components used in extreme temperature environments (like cryogenic tanks or high-temperature furnaces). Materials are selected and analyzed to ensure it handles stresses without cracking or deforming under temperature extremes. What Are the Units of Stress? The units of stress are listed below. Pascal (Pa) : The pascal is the SI unit of stress, defined as one newton of force per square meter of area (1 Pa = 1 N/m²). Most structural and mechanical engineering analyses outside North America use megapascals (MPa), where 1 MPa equals 1 N/mm², and gigapascals (GPa) for very high-stiffness applications. Steel's yield strength, for example, falls in the range of 250 MPa to 690 MPa. Pounds per Square Inch (psi) : The psi is the customary unit used in American engineering practice, defined as one pound-force acting on one square inch of area. High-strength structural steel carries a tensile strength of approximately 58,000 psi to 100,000 psi in standard ASTM grades. Kilopounds per square inch (ksi) is used for values exceeding 1,000 psi. Megapascal (MPa) : The megapascal is the practical working unit for most solid mechanics problems because material strengths fall conveniently into the range of tens to hundreds of MPa. A conversion factor of 1 MPa = 145.04 psi allows direct comparison from SI to imperial values. Gigapascal (GPa): GPa is commonly used for elastic modulus and very high stress values, but it is not exclusively reserved for those applications. The elastic modulus of structural steel is 200 GPa, while diamond’s Young’s modulus is approximately 1,00–1,200 GPa, depending on crystal orientation and measurement method. Bar and Atmosphere (atm) : The bar and atm units appear in pressure and fluid mechanics contexts but are occasionally cited in stress references. One bar equals 0.1 MPa, and one atm equals approximately 0.101 MPa, making it roughly equivalent for order-of-magnitude stress estimation. How Is Stress Measured in Mechanics? Stress is measured in Mechanics by following the six steps below. Define the Loading Conditions . Identify all forces, moments, pressures, and thermal loads acting on the component, including their magnitudes, directions, and points of application. Accurate load definition, gathered from load cells, pressure transducers, or force plates, is the prerequisite for any valid stress calculation. Establish the Geometry and Cross-Section . Measure the cross-sectional dimensions at the critical location using calipers, coordinate measuring machines (CMMs), or 3D scanning. For simple direct stress calculations using σ = F/A, a 1% error in cross-sectional area produces a corresponding 1% error in calculated stress. This direct proportionality does not generally apply to bending, torsion, multiaxial stress states, or finite element analysis (FEA), where stress depends on additional factors such as moment of inertia, section modulus, stress concentrations, boundary conditions, and mesh quality. Apply Strain Gauges . Bond resistance strain gauges to the surface of the component at locations where stress is expected to peak. A strain gauge measures the fractional change in electrical resistance caused by surface strain; combined with the material's elastic modulus, the measured strain converts directly to surface stress through Hooke's law (σ = Eε). Conduct Photoelastic Analysis . Load a transparent model of the component made from a birefringent polymer (epoxy, polycarbonate) and illuminate it with polarized light. The resulting fringe pattern reveals the full-field shear stress distribution visually, with fringe density proportional to stress magnitude. Perform Finite Element Analysis (FEA) . Build a computational mesh of the component geometry, assign material properties, apply boundary conditions, and solve the system of equations to obtain the stress field at every element. FEA identifies peak stresses at geometric features (fillets, holes, threads) that analytical formulas do not capture. Apply X-ray or Neutron Diffraction . Measure lattice spacing in crystalline materials using X-ray or neutron diffraction to determine residual stresses trapped within a part from manufacturing processes. The shift in diffraction peak position corresponds directly to elastic strain, and Hooke's law converts that strain to residual stress. Why Does the Stress of Materials Need To Be Measured? The stress of materials needs to be measured because analytical predictions alone carry assumptions (uniform material properties, idealized geometry, simplified loading) that real components violate. A weld joint, for example, contains a heat-affected zone with different yield strength, residual tensile stress from solidification shrinkage, and geometric irregularities at the toe, none of which appear in a textbook beam formula. The actual stress state at that weld remains unknown without measurement, and the designer cannot confirm whether the safety factor assumed in the design is maintained in the manufactured part. Regulatory bodies require documented stress measurement data for pressure vessels (ASME Section VIII), nuclear components (ASME Section III), and aircraft structures (FAR 25) before approving the component for service. Measurement detects unexpected stress concentrations caused by manufacturing defects (porosity, inclusions, tool marks) that appear only after production. The combination of predictive analysis and direct measurement provides the verification needed to release a component into service with confidence. What Are the Effects of Stress on Materials? Stress produces a range of physical effects on materials depending on its magnitude, type, and duration relative to the material's inherent properties. A material deforms proportionally to the applied load and recovers its original dimensions fully when the load is removed at low stress levels, within the elastic range. Permanent plastic deformation begins as stress reaches the yield strength. A mild steel bar with a yield strength of 250 MPa retains a permanent set after stress exceeds that threshold. Stress levels near the ultimate tensile strength, necking, and fracture occur, ending the component's useful life. Cyclic stresses below the yield strength cause fatigue damage through progressive crack growth. A crack initiated at a surface scratch propagates at rates measurable in micrometers per cycle until the remaining cross-section no longer carries the load. Sustained stress causes creep at elevated temperatures, a time-dependent plastic flow that occurs even below the yield strength. Nickel superalloys in gas turbine blades creep measurably at operating temperatures above 800°C. Fracture toughness is not a stress threshold; it relates applied stress to crack size through stress intensity. What Are the Benefits of Stress Analysis in Materials? The benefits of stress analysis in materials deliver quantifiable engineering that reduces cost, extends service life, and prevents failure. Identifying peak stress locations during the design phase allows engineers to add material only where needed, reducing component weight without compromising strength. In aerospace structures, fuel savings per kilogram vary widely by aircraft type, route, utilization, and operating profile; a fixed 3,000-liter value is not universally valid. Stress analysis enables the optimization of heat treatment parameters, knowing that a gear tooth root experiences bending stress of 600 MPa, which guides the specification of a case-hardening depth that places the compressive residual stress layer precisely at the highest-stressed location. Predictive fatigue life analysis, based on stress amplitude data, schedules inspection intervals before cracks reach critical size, keeping components in service longer and reducing unplanned downtime. Stress analysis of printed parts identifies the build orientation that minimizes residual thermal stress and warping during cooling in additive manufacturing. Structural health monitoring systems use real-time stress data from embedded sensors to track cumulative fatigue damage in bridges, wind turbine towers, and offshore platforms, allowing maintenance to occur based on actual loading history instead of fixed calendar intervals. What Are the Limitations of Stress Analysis in Materials? The limitations of stress analysis in materials are primarily due to simplifying assumptions, material behavior complexities, and external factors that affect accuracy. Analytical stress formulas assume idealized geometries, homogeneous material properties, and simplified loading conditions that manufactured parts rarely satisfy exactly. Finite element analysis produces results only as accurate as the input material data, mesh density, and boundary conditions allow; an incorrectly specified contact condition at a bolted joint, for example, generates stress results that differ from physical reality by 30% or more. Material property data used in stress analysis (yield strength, fracture toughness, fatigue limit) represent average values from standardized test specimens, not the specific microstructure of every production part. Residual stresses from welding, machining, and heat treatment are difficult to quantify without expensive diffraction measurements, yet they add directly to applied stress. Stress analysis alone cannot predict failure modes driven by environmental factors (corrosion, hydrogen embrittlement, radiation damage) without coupling to separate degradation models. Engineers treat stress analysis results as engineering estimates carrying inherent uncertainty instead of exact predictions. What Is the Formula of Stress? The fundamental formula of stress is σ = F/A, where σ represents normal stress in pascals (Pa), F is the applied normal force in newtons (N), and A is the cross-sectional area in square meters (m²). The normal stress equals 200 MPa for a circular rod with a diameter of 20 mm (area = 314.16 mm²) carrying an axial tensile load of 62,832 N. Shear stress uses the analogous formula τ = V/A, where V is the shear force acting parallel to the cross-section. Bending stress follows the flexure formula σ = Mc/I, where M is the bending moment, c is the distance from the neutral axis to the outermost fiber, and I is the second moment of area of the cross-section. Torsional shear stress is given by τ = Tr/J, where T is the applied torque, r is the radial distance from the shaft center, and J is the polar moment of inertia. The stress tensor combines all components into a 3x3 matrix that fully describes the stress state at a point. How Is the Stress-Strain Relationship Significant in Mechanics? The stress-strain relationship is significant in mechanics because it defines how a material responds mechanically to every level of applied stress, from elastic deformation through plastic flow to final fracture. In the elastic region, stress and strain are proportional, governed by Hooke's law (σ = Eε), where E is Young's modulus. Structural steel has a Young's modulus of 200 GPa, meaning it produces an elastic strain of approximately 0.001, assuming linear-elastic behavior and E = 200 GPa, or 0.1% elongation per unit length. The yield point on the stress-strain curve marks the transition from recoverable to permanent deformation, while the area under the curve up to fracture represents the modulus of toughness, measuring the total energy the material absorbs before failure. A high-toughness material (low-alloy steel) absorbs more energy than a brittle ceramic at the same strength level. The stress-strain curve also reveals the strain-hardening behavior of a material, where continued plastic deformation increases the flow stress, enabling processes (cold drawing, rolling, stamping) that strengthen the material during shaping. The full characterization of a material's mechanical behavior from elastic modulus through fracture strain is captured in the Stress vs. Strain relationship plotted from standardized tensile testing. What Are Some Stress-Related Failure Modes? Some stress-related failure modes are listed below. Yielding : Yielding occurs when applied stress exceeds the material's yield strength, producing permanent plastic deformation that alters the component's dimensions and fit. A steel shaft that yields under overload bends permanently and no longer rotates concentrically within its bearings. Brittle Fracture : Brittle fracture occurs suddenly when stress at a crack tip exceeds the material's fracture toughness (KIc), with no preceding plastic deformation as a warning. Cast iron, hardened steel, and glass are susceptible materials; the Liberty Ship failures during World War II resulted from brittle fracture of welded steel hull plates at low temperatures. Fatigue Failure: Fatigue failure results from the initiation and propagation of a crack under cyclic stress amplitudes below the static yield strength. Fatigue is widely reported as a major cause of mechanical failure, often cited in the range of roughly 50%-90% depending on industry and study. Creep Rupture : Creep rupture occurs when a material subjected to sustained stress at elevated temperatures slowly deforms over time until fracture. Steam turbine blades and furnace components operating above 50% of the material's melting point in kelvin are the primary applications where creep rupture governs design. Stress Corrosion Cracking (SCC) : Stress corrosion cracking results from the simultaneous action of sustained tensile stress and a corrosive environment, producing crack growth at stress levels well below the yield strength. Stainless steel in chloride environments, brass in ammonia, and high-strength aluminum in saltwater all exhibit SCC under service conditions. Plastic Deformation : Plastic deformation occurs when stress exceeds the material's yield strength, causing irreversible changes to the material’s shape. Plastic deformation leads to a reduction in strength over time as the material undergoes deformation that affects its ability to handle future loads, while yielding leads to permanent changes. Tensile Rupture : Tensile rupture happens when a material subjected to excessive tensile stress reaches a point of failure, typically under sudden, large forces. Tensile rupture is seen in materials such as polymers and thin metals, which experience rapid fracture when stretched beyond their tensile strength. Buckling : Buckling occurs when compressive stress exceeds the critical load-bearing capacity of a slender structure, causing it to bend or collapse. Columns and structural beams are common components susceptible to buckling when subjected to excessive axial compressive stress. Wear: Wear results from surface interaction mechanisms such as friction, abrasion, adhesion, erosion, or contact fatigue. Common in mechanical components like gears, bearings, and joints, wear leads to material loss, dimensional changes, and eventual failure. Thermal Fatigue : Thermal fatigue occurs when a material is subjected to repeated temperature cycles, causing expansion and contraction that leads to stress buildup. The thermal stresses can initiate cracks, particularly in materials like metals and ceramics exposed to rapid heating and cooling. Impact Fracture : Impact fracture occurs when a material is subjected to a high-stress impact load that exceeds its fracture toughness. The type of failure is often abrupt and causes catastrophic damage, especially in brittle materials subjected to sudden impacts, such as in automotive collisions or machinery failures. Delamination : Delamination refers to the separation of layers in composite materials due to stress. Delamination is seen in materials like laminated plastics or carbon fiber composites, where the bond between layers is weak under tensile or shear stress, leading to a failure mode that severely reduces the material’s integrity. What Is the Difference Between Tensile Stress and Compressive Stress? The difference between tensile stress and compressive stress lies in the direction of the applied forces and the resulting material deformation. Tensile stress and compressive stress are normal stresses acting perpendicular to a cross-section, but differ in direction and effect on the material. Tensile stress pulls the cross-section apart, elongating the member along its loaded axis and reducing its cross-sectional area through the Poisson effect. Compressive stress pushes the cross-section together, shortening the member and increasing its cross-sectional area. Ductile metals (structural steel, aluminum) resist tensile and compressive stress with roughly equal yield strengths. The tensile yield strength of ASTM A36 steel is 250 MPa, and its compressive yield strength is effectively the same. Brittle materials (concrete, cast iron, ceramics) exhibit a pronounced asymmetry against concrete, with a compressive strength of 30 MPa carries a tensile strength of only 2 MPa to 5 MPa. The asymmetry explains why concrete structures require steel reinforcement at the tensile faces of beams. The sign convention assigns positive values to tensile stress and negative values to compressive stress in standard mechanics notation. What Is the Difference Between Normal Stress and Shear Stress? The difference lies in the direction of the stress relative to a plane or cross-sectional area within the material. Normal stress acts perpendicular to the cross-sectional plane, either pulling (tension) or pushing (compression) the material along the axis of the applied force. Shear stress acts parallel to the cross-sectional plane, tending to slide one layer of material relative to the adjacent layer. A bolted lap joint illustrates the distinction clearly: the bolt shank carries shear stress on the plane where the two plates overlap, while the bolt threads and clamped plates carry tensile normal stress along the bolt axis. Normal stress is calculated as σ = F/A for axial loads, while shear stress is calculated as τ = V/A for direct shear or τ = Tr/J for torsion. Failure theories treat normal and shear stress differently. The von Mises criterion combines normal and shear into an equivalent stress, while the maximum normal stress criterion ignores shear entirely, making theory selection critical for accurate failure prediction. What Are the Causes of Stress in Materials? The causes of stress in materials are listed below. Mechanical Loading: Applied forces (point loads, distributed loads, pressure) are the most direct cause of stress. The nominal compressive stress is 5,000 MPa, assuming uniform load distribution over the full contact area. Thermal Expansion and Contraction : Temperature changes cause materials to expand or contract. Internal thermal stress develops equal to E × α × ΔT when a constrained component does not deform freely, where α is the coefficient of thermal expansion, and ΔT is the temperature change. A steel pipe constrained from expanding through a 100°C temperature rise develops a thermal stress of approximately 200 MPa. Residual Stress from Manufacturing : Welding, casting, quenching, and machining introduce residual stresses that remain in the part after processing is complete. Weld shrinkage routinely generates residual tensile stresses at the weld toe approaching the material's yield strength, up to 350 MPa in low-alloy steel weldments. Dynamic and Impact Loading : Rapidly applied loads generate stress waves that travel through a material at the speed of sound. Impact stress can be 2 to 10 times the equivalent static stress, depending on the loading rate and material damping characteristics. Centrifugal Forces : Rotating components (turbine discs, flywheels, impellers) generate centrifugal body forces that produce hoop and radial stresses proportional to the square of the rotational speed. A steel flywheel rotating at 3,000 RPM develops hoop stresses that increase by a factor of 4 if speed doubles to 6,000 RPM. Gravitational Self-Weight : Large structures (bridges, dams, tall buildings) carry significant stress from the weight of the structure itself. The base columns of a 300-meter-tall steel building carry axial compressive stresses from self-weight alone that routinely reach 100 MPa to 150 MPa, before any live load is applied. How Do External Loads Create Internal Stress? External loads create internal stress by requiring the material's internal cross-sections to carry forces that maintain static equilibrium throughout the body. Every cross-section from support to load point must carry a shear force and bending moment that balances the applied load and support reactions simultaneously when a beam rests on two supports and carries a central point load of 10 kN. The internal force at any cross-section is not concentrated at a single point but distributed continuously across the area, with the stress at each location determined by the force intensity per unit area at that point. The load path narrows at geometric transitions (shoulder fillets, holes, keyways), forcing the distributed internal force through a smaller area and elevating local stress by a factor quantified by the stress concentration factor Kt. The local stress at the hole edge reaches 3 times the nominal far-field stress in a plate with a central circular hole under uniaxial tension, a well-established result from elasticity theory. The force transmission mechanism operates identically in metals, polymers, ceramics, and composites, though the magnitude of stress concentration and the failure mode vary with material properties. Can Temperature and Loads Both Cause Stress? Yes, temperature changes and mechanical loads cause stress, and act simultaneously in most real engineering components. A gas turbine blade, for example, carries centrifugal tensile stress from rotation, bending stress from aerodynamic pressure on the airfoil, and thermal stress from the temperature gradient from the hot gas path (above 900°C) to the cooled blade root. The stresses from each source add algebraically at every point where thermal and mechanical stresses are tensile and act in the same direction. The combined stress exceeds either source alone. Solder joints experience mechanical stress from board flexure during handling and thermal stress from cyclic heating during operation in printed circuit boards, with the combined cyclic loading governing solder fatigue life. The coupling of thermal and mechanical stress is addressed in thermo-mechanical fatigue (TMF) analysis, a specialized discipline that accounts for the phase relationship between mechanical and thermal cycle peaks. Ignoring thermal stress in a mechanically loaded structure consistently produces unconservative designs. What 3D Printing Materials Handle Mechanical Stress? The 3D printing materials that handle mechanical stress are listed below. Nylon (PA12, PA11) : Nylon handles tensile stresses from 40 MPa to 80 MPa, depending on the printing process (SLS vs. FDM) and print orientation. Its high elongation at break (15% to 50% for SLS parts) makes it resistant to impact and fatigue loading encountered in snap-fit assemblies and living hinges. Polycarbonate (PC) : Polycarbonate reaches tensile strengths from 55 MPa to 70 MPa in FDM-printed parts, with good resistance to impact stress. The material retains structural integrity at temperatures up to 110°C, making it suitable for under-hood automotive components and electrical housings that experience combined thermal and mechanical stress. PEEK (Polyether Ether Ketone) : PEEK carries tensile stresses from 80 MPa to 100 MPa in FDM-printed parts and up to 200 MPa in machined form. PEEK is a widely used high-performance polymer in medical and aerospace applications, but “dominant” is too broad and application-dependent. Carbon Fiber Reinforced Nylon (CF-Nylon) : Carbon fiber reinforced nylon achieves tensile strengths from 120 MPa to 200 MPa along the fiber direction, outperforming unreinforced nylon by a factor of 2 to 3. The reinforcement is directional, meaning stress resistance is highest along the fiber axis and significantly lower perpendicular to it. Ti-6Al-4V (Titanium Alloy, LPBF) : Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) printed Ti-6Al-4V achieves tensile strengths from 900 MPa to 1,050 MPa after heat treatment, matching or exceeding wrought equivalents for most orientations. Aerospace and medical implant applications rely on printed titanium for its high strength-to-weight ratio under sustained mechanical stress. summary: How to Build an AI Agent for Customer Service That Remembers Across Phone, Email, and Chat
body_text: Quick Takeaways: 73% of customers expect to move between channels without having to repeat themselves. 53% of consumers say they always have to repeat their issue when transferred between agents. The fix is one shared user_id in Mem0 that all channel endpoints write to and read from. Channel identity is a routing concern. Memory identity is unified. Mem0's scoping model ( user_id , agent_id , run_id ) gives you precise control: cross-channel facts live at user_id scope, session state lives at run_id scope, and per-channel behavior tuning lives at agent_id scope. The demo in this post is a FastAPI backend with three endpoints ( POST /call , POST /email , POST /chat ) and a Streamlit UI, all reading and writing the same memory store, with the customer's email as the shared key. Memory extracted from a phone transcript is available in the next chat session automatically. 💡 You'll need a free Mem0 API key to follow along. Get one at app.mem0.ai Here is the scenario : A customer calls your support line, explains their billing issue for four minutes, and resolves the call. Three days later, they email about a receipt. The agent asks them to describe the issue again. That is what happens when your channels don't share memory. 73% of customers expect to start on one channel and finish on another without repeating themselves( survey ). 53% of consumers say they always have to repeat their issue when transferred between agents. Only 13% of companies report that customer data, history, and context carry over fully across interactions and channels ( Deloitte's 2024 GCS survey ). The standard response is to invest in a unified CRM dashboard, give agents a better inbox, and call it omnichannel. This kind of system does nothing for the AI agent generating the response in real time. In this blog, we’ll understand that whether you're building an AI customer service bot or a full agent pipeline, you'll end up with a FastAPI backend, three or more channel endpoints, and a Streamlit UI that all read and write the same Mem0 memory store. Here is a glimpse of what we’ll build: Please enter a valid YouTube, Vimeo, or direct video URL 💡 You can review the full code on the GitHub repository. Why siloed channels produce bad AI customer support agents Most support architectures are multichannel, not omnichannel customer support. They're available on multiple platforms (email, chat, phone), but each channel runs its own stack. Its own queue, its own agent prompt, and its own history store. When a customer switches, they're starting over. The difference between multichannel and omnichannel is whether context moves with the customer. In 2026, the main failure point is no longer channel access . It's channel switching. Customers can usually find a way in. The problem is what happens when they move from a phone call to an email to a chat. If the AI agent only sees the current channel and not the customer's history across all channels, it asks redundant questions, misses prior resolutions, and starts fresh every time. This is a memory architecture problem. A bigger context window doesn't solve the cross-session problem: even 1M tokens only helps if the right history is in the window. When a customer switches channels, there's no guarantee any prior history is present at all. Four specific things break when channels are siloed: Re-asking: The agent asks for information the customer already gave on another channel. This is the 53% problem. Context mismatch: The email agent refers to a billing status the phone agent already resolved. Tone drift: The phone call was urgent and empathetic. The chatbot reply is formal and generic. The customer feels like they're talking to a different company. Duplicate escalations: The chat agent escalates an issue the phone agent already escalated. Engineering gets two tickets about the same problem. The fix is conceptually simple: Give every channel endpoint the same identity key and the same memory store. When the phone call ends, extract the facts. When the email comes in, extract more. When the chat opens, retrieve everything relevant. One user_id , all channels, shared retrieval. How does Mem0 scope memory across channels? Mem0 's scoping model maps onto a multi-channel support use case. There are four identity dimensions available on every add() and search() call. user_id is the cross-channel with cross-session scope. Facts stored here persist across every channel and every session for the user. This is where cross-channel support memory lives: "user is on the annual plan," "payment failed on May 14," "needs receipt for expense report." Use the customer's email as the user_id so it resolves naturally across channels regardless of which one the customer used to contact you. agent_id is the per-channel-agent scope. The phone agent, email agent, and chat agent each get their own agent_id . We pass it for agent-level provenance, but note that combining user_id and agent_id filters in a single search() call can be tricky. For the practical channel audit trail, metadata={"channel": channel} is the more reliable tag. run_id is the session scope. It is useful for scoping a single conversation in-progress state, or for cleaning up a session's temporary context after it closes. Pass a run_id per session if you need to isolate or expire session-level facts. app_id is the application-level scope. It is used ****for shared organizational context like product catalog, policy documents, and known bugs. Not used in this demo but useful in production when you want all agents to share institutional knowledge. For a multi-channel support agent, the practical mapping looks like this: Scope What you store Example user_id Cross-channel facts "Annual plan, card 4821, $199 charge, May 14" agent_id Agent-level provenance Phone vs email vs chat agent. Use metadata.channel for audit queries run_id In-session ephemeral state Current chat session, this call's draft response app_id Org-wide shared knowledge Refund policy, known billing bugs, escalation paths One important constraint to know before writing any queries : Mem0's search() requires entity parameters inside a filters={} dict, not as top-level keyword arguments. For cross-channel retrieval, always query at user_id scope. # Correct: entity params inside filters={} result = mem0 . search ( query , filters = { "user_id" : user_id } , top_k = 6 ) # Wrong: will raise ValueError at runtime result = mem0 . search ( query , user_id = user_id , top_k = 6 ) # ValidationError # Correct: entity params inside filters={} result = mem0 . search ( query , filters = { "user_id" : user_id } , top_k = 6 ) # Wrong: will raise ValueError at runtime result = mem0 . search ( query , user_id = user_id , top_k = 6 ) # ValidationError # Correct: entity params inside filters={} result = mem0 . search ( query , filters = { "user_id" : user_id } , top_k = 6 ) # Wrong: will raise ValueError at runtime result = mem0 . search ( query , user_id = user_id , top_k = 6 ) # ValidationError 💡 The multi-agent memory systems post documents the scoping model in full detail. Worth reading before you build anything beyond a single-agent setup. The Architecture The architecture has two layers. A FastAPI backend exposes three endpoints. A Streamlit UI runs the demo with a tab per channel. All three endpoints share the same user_id (the customer's email) and the same Mem0 memory store. The customer's email is the shared memory key. The phone agent extracts it from the call transcript. The email agent reads it from the From: header. The chat agent asks for it on first contact, then uses it for all subsequent memory reads and writes. In production, this runs before every agent response across every channel. Start free on Mem0 and store your first memories for free. The metadata={"channel": channel} tag on every write is worth noting. It doesn't affect retrieval ( search() ignores metadata by default), but it lets you audit which channel contributed which facts in the Mem0 dashboard. One note on the V3 API: add() can return an async queued response with status and event_id rather than a results list. The demo uses result.get("results", []) as a safe fallback, but don't rely on a memory count for production logic. Second, Mem0 runs its own extraction over the message content and stores the facts worth keeping: plan type, payment amounts, card details, stated constraints, emotional context. The distinction matters: Your app resolves identity, Mem0 extracts memory facts. You don't write extraction rules for either. POST /email - Ingest an inbound support email This step receives an inbound support email where the subject and body are combined, so Mem0 extracts intent from both. The customer_email is used as user_id for cross-channel memory. @ app . post ( "/email" , response_model = MemoryResponse ) def handle_email ( req : EmailRequest ) : combined = f"Subject: { req . subject } \\n\\n { req . body } " messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : combined } ] stored = store_memories ( messages = messages , user_id = req . customer_email . lower ( ) , # email as the shared key agent_id = EMAIL_AGENT_ID , run_id = req . run_id , channel = "email" , ) return MemoryResponse ( status = "ok" , memories_stored = stored , message = f"Email processed. { stored } memories extracted." , ) @ app . post ( "/email" , response_model = MemoryResponse ) def handle_email ( req : EmailRequest ) : combined = f"Subject: { req . subject } \\n\\n { req . body } " messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : combined } ] stored = store_memories ( messages = messages , user_id = req . customer_email . lower ( ) , # email as the shared key agent_id = EMAIL_AGENT_ID , run_id = req . run_id , channel = "email" , ) return MemoryResponse ( status = "ok" , memories_stored = stored , message = f"Email processed. { stored } memories extracted." , ) @ app . post ( "/email" , response_model = MemoryResponse ) def handle_email ( req : EmailRequest ) : combined = f"Subject: { req . subject } \\n\\n { req . body } " messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : combined } ] stored = store_memories ( messages = messages , user_id = req . customer_email . lower ( ) , # email as the shared key agent_id = EMAIL_AGENT_ID , run_id = req . run_id , channel = "email" , ) return MemoryResponse ( status = "ok" , memories_stored = stored , message = f"Email processed. { stored } memories extracted." , ) The customer_email.lower() normalization matters. [email protected] and [email protected] would resolve to different user_id s in Mem0 without it. Thus, we lowercase everything before storing. It retrieves all prior memory across channels before generating a response, then stores the new turn for future channels to see. Here is how we implement real-time chat turn: 1. Ask for email on first turn if not already known. 2. Retrieve cross-channel memories scoped to this user. 3. Build memory-augmented system prompt. 4. Generate response. 5.
